summary:
AFTERLIFE OF SPACE is an interactive digital museum we created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to bridge the emotional gap between complex planetary data and young, curious minds.

Addressing the Challenge & Using Open NASA Data:
NASA’s challenge asks us to uncover the forgotten stories of hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars. Instead of showing static spreadsheets, we transform authentic open-source NASA resources—including Planetary Data System (PDS) telemetry, LROC/MOLA elevation maps, NSSDC spacecraft catalogs, and live photography from the NASA Image and Video Library API—into living, first-person narratives.

Key Features & Educational Impact:
Learners step into the shoes of Space Archaeologists using our Dual-World Radar, Wake the Machine voice monologues, In-Character AI Chat, visual Science Discovery Pipelines, a 1967–Present Timeline, and XP Ranks. By giving silent equipment a voice backed by real science, we turn discarded machines into inspiring, hands-on STEM classrooms that ignite a passion for future space exploration.
details:
AFTERLIFE OF SPACE is an interactive planetary archaeology museum that transforms neglected Moon and Mars hardware into living, first-person stories. It works by streaming authentic open-source NASA data through a dual-world topographic radar, an 8-machine archive, and typewriter voice monologues.

The project delivers profound educational benefits by sparking curiosity and grounding imagination in genuine PDS and LROC datasets. Its intended impact is to inspire the next generation of scientists, transforming dry telemetry into a captivating STEM journey.

Built entirely as a zero-backend, high-performance web application, our tech stack relies on semantic HTML, utility-first Tailwind CSS, minimalist Bootstrap grid components, and robust inline JavaScript for real-time radar rendering and Web Speech audio.

Our team’s creativity shines through its gamified Space Archaeologist XP progression, AI chat relays, and the emotional "Wake the Machine" mechanic. In designing it, we carefully considered accessibility, historical accuracy, and strict adherence to NASA open data provenance guidelines, ensuring an engaging, educational experience.
